title: Atlas of Questions
premise: Follow records, arguments and instruments as they are translated, challenged and put to new work—then combine them into explicitly speculative future laboratories, shared memories and living cities. Historical chapters are dated teaching reconstructions, not an inevitable march toward truth; the future inventions are fiction, not forecasts.

items.label: Blank tablet for a dated sky report
items.description: A blank writing surface.

items.label: Reed stylus
items.description: A reusable writing tool.

items.label: Lunar month counts: 1, 7, 13
items.description: The counts refer to elapsed lunar months, not repeating month names.

reading.text: For this small invented exercise, number consecutive lunar months 1, 2, 3, and so on. The three entries of interest are in months 1, 7 and 13. These are teaching numbers, not dates transcribed from an ancient tablet.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Month 13: eclipse seen; 14: clouded; 15: missed
items.description: A particular dated observation dossier.

reading.text: At the full Moon of month 13 an eclipse was seen. Cloud hid the Moon during the relevant watch in month 14. Nobody attended the watch in month 15. The last two entries do not record an uneclipsed Moon.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Earlier eclipses: months 1 and 7
items.description: Earlier reports of seen lunar eclipses.

reading.text: Both earlier reports describe a seen eclipse. This schematic six-month sample makes subtraction and recurrence visible; it is not a reconstruction of a complete Babylonian prediction algorithm. Actual eclipse opportunities are not a guarantee of a locally visible eclipse.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Future full Moons: months 16, 17, 18, 19
items.description: A calendar strip on which a further watch can be marked.

items.label: For the king: an eclipse threatens his reign
items.description: A fictional omen interpretation, not a physical cause of darkening.

reading.text: This invented omen wording stands for divinatory interpretation. Celestial records and political or religious meaning could coexist in Mesopotamian scholarship. The observer can report what was seen without erasing the interpreter’s concern.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Ruled tablet for a dated sky report
items.description: The writing surface is ruled for entries.

items.label: Dated eclipse tablet
items.description: The tablet carries the particular observation and the two gaps.

reading.text: Month 13: an eclipse was seen. Month 14: the sky was clouded. Month 15: the watch was missed. These are three different records, not three claims that the Moon was uneclipsed.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Month reckoning: 7−1=6; 13−7=6
items.description: A numerical reference for the two intervals. The reference survives its astronomical use.

items.label: Seen eclipses: months 1, 7 and 13
items.description: The present tablet is placed alongside the two earlier reports.

items.label: Eclipse watches recur six months apart
items.description: The three dated reports support a six-month watching pattern in this schematic case.

reading.text: The observed entries are separated by six months. This is a reason to appoint another watch, not a claim that every sixth full Moon must produce a visible eclipse. Babylonian eclipse prediction was more elaborate than this exercise.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Earlier pair: six months between eclipses
items.description: The subtraction is first applied to the two old reports.

items.label: Watch the full Moon in month 19
items.description: The next six-month opportunity is marked on the future calendar.

items.label: King’s report: the eclipse and its omen
items.description: The report brings the observed event and its proposed significance to the king; neither is silently substituted for the other.

reading.text: The tablet reports a seen eclipse in month 13, followed by a clouded watch and a missed watch. The accompanying interpretation warns the king. The report contains both statements without presenting the interpretation as the observation.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Every darkening is caused by a cover
items.description: A sweeping premise offered by a fictional speaker.

reading.text: The speaker’s universal claim ranges over all darkenings, not only eclipses. It can be put into a valid inference even if that sweeping premise is false. Aristotle’s eclipse discussions supply the setting, not these invented words.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Every A is B; this is A; so this is B
items.description: A compact modern rendering of a deductive pattern.

reading.text: This form preserves the conclusion if the premises hold. It does not establish the premises. The letters are modern teaching shorthand for a family of ancient deductive arguments.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: An uncovered lamp darkens as its oil runs out
items.description: A particular case in which darkening occurs without a covering body.

items.label: Earth screens the light—or the Moon itself changes
items.description: Two teaching accounts with an agreed eclipse prediction.

reading.text: Aristotle, Posterior Analytics II.8, contrasts possible explanations involving Earth as a screen, lunar rotation, or extinction while discussing the search for a cause. These two simplified speakers and their identical forecast are invented; no real ancient astronomer is credited with this toy predictive model.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Month 19: the Moon darkens; no cause is seen
items.description: The observed outcome at the appointed watch.

reading.text: The new watcher records a darkening at the predicted watch. This outcome alone is shared by the two teaching accounts. It neither establishes that all darkening involves a cover nor chooses between those accounts.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: The Moon darkened; every darkening supposedly has a cover
items.description: The observed particular and the speaker’s universal premise are now side by side.

items.label: If those premises hold, the Moon had a cover
items.description: The inference is valid; its universal premise remains an assertive, challengeable claim.

reading.text: The form is: every A is B; this is A; therefore this is B. Here A is darkening and B is being caused by a cover. A valid form does not make the speaker’s universal premise true. The same distinction between premises and entailment can be reused with mathematical statements.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Under that premise, any darkening implies a cover
items.description: The rule is arranged before a particular recorded case is supplied.

items.label: One uncovered lamp breaks the “every darkening” claim
items.description: The single case defeats this universal premise, not all accounts of eclipses.

reading.text: The lamp darkens without being covered. Thus it contradicts the claim that every darkening is caused by a cover. The reusable argument is that one genuine contrary case defeats an unrestricted universal statement; it need not defeat a narrower claim.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Both accounts predict a dark Moon in month 19
items.description: The rival accounts make the same prediction at the calendar’s appointed watch.

items.label: One observed dark Moon fits both rival accounts
items.description: This observation answers the shared prediction; the accounts are still distinct.

reading.text: Both teaching accounts predicted this same darkening, and it occurred. The observation therefore does not select one account over the other. Another observation could do more if their predictions differ. This case can later help distinguish a successful representation from a uniquely established cause.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Straightedge
items.description: A reusable tool for joining the constructed points.

items.label: Compass set to length AB
items.description: Draws circles with the given segment as radius.

items.label: Segment AB: construct three equal sides
items.description: The given side of the desired equilateral triangle.

items.label: Every radius of a circle has the same length
items.description: A mathematical premise rather than a ruler measurement.

reading.text: The points of a circle have equal distance from its centre. In the construction, one circle is centred at A with radius AB; the other is centred at B with radius BA. The notation is a compact teaching rendering of Euclid I.1.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Lengths equal to AB are equal to each other
items.description: The equality premise needed to connect the two circles.

items.label: Copy A: circles meet at C; join AC and BC
items.description: An invented textual witness with a consistent vertex name.

reading.text: This teaching witness names the intersection C and tells the reader to join AC and BC. It leaves the justification incomplete. It is not an actual ancient manuscript.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Copy B: circles meet at D; join AC and BC
items.description: An invented copy with a particular inconsistent vertex name.

reading.text: This teaching witness names the intersection D but then tells the reader to join AC and BC, without defining C. The conflict is a copying problem. Nothing here asserts that renaming all occurrences consistently from C to D would be a geometric error.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: “Every equal-looking triangle is equilateral”: sides 5, 5, 6
items.description: A claim attached to a sketch with explicitly unequal side lengths.

items.label: Circles centred at A and B, both with radius AB
items.description: The two circles provide an intersection C in the Euclidean plane.

items.label: Triangle ABC: join A and B to the circle intersection
items.description: The sides have been drawn from the actual construction.

items.label: AC=AB in one circle; BC=AB in the other
items.description: The construction, not the sketch’s apparent proportions, warrants these equalities.

items.label: AC=AB and BC=AB; equal to one length means equal
items.description: The equalities and the equality premise are assembled.

items.label: AC=AB=BC: the constructed triangle has three equal sides
items.description: The mathematical conclusion follows from the specified premises.

reading.text: Each circle has radius AB. Thus AC equals AB, and BC equals AB. Since both equal AB, all three sides are equal. This reconstructs the core of Euclid I.1 in the Euclidean plane, not a claim that every later foundation of geometry leaves its assumptions unchallenged.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: The 5–5–6 triangle defeats “equal-looking means equilateral”
items.description: A genuine contrary case overturns the sketch’s universal claim, not the circle construction.

items.label: One copy says C; the other leaves C undefined
items.description: The exact disagreement remains visible.

items.label: C restored at the intersection; the D reading is recorded
items.description: The construction supplies the missing referent without concealing the rival reading.

reading.text: At the circles’ intersection the edited teaching text uses C, so its instructions to draw AC and BC have a defined endpoint. The alternate D reading is recorded alongside the repair. Consistently renaming the point would also preserve the geometry; this particular copy had not done so.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

items.label: Triangle proof: three equal sides, vertex C restored
items.description: The completed roll contains the construction, its proof, and the particular repaired reading.

sources.title: NASA/JPL: AEGIS autonomous science targeting
sources.note: Actual bounded target-selection autonomy. It is not evidence that the fictional self-questioning laboratory exists.

sources.title: Francesca Schironi: Textual Scholarship in Alexandria and Beyond
sources.note: Scholar-authored research on textual practices. Modern apparatus and translation terms in this game are not all ancient Alexandrian inventions.

sources.title: Oxford History of Science Museum: mathematics in Islamic cultures
sources.note: Practical problems, inherited mathematics and original contributions cross languages and regions. No exclusive origin claim.

sources.title: Influence of Arabic and Islamic Philosophy on the Latin West, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
Aristotle: Prior Analytics, translated primary text
sources.note: Ancient syllogistic; modern symbolic notation and toy examples are explanatory reconstructions.

sources.title: Francesca Rochberg, Science and Ancient Mesopotamia, Cambridge History of Science
George Boole: An Investigation of the Laws of Thought (1854)
sources.note: Primary historical text; binary gate notation is a modern teaching representation.

sources.title: Eduard Buchner, Alcoholic Fermentation Without Yeast Cells (1897), translated primary text
Eleanor Robson: Digital Corpus of Cuneiform Mathematical Texts
sources.note: Scribal arithmetic and numerical records; game quantities are invented, not translated tablets.

sources.title: Charles Darwin, Recollections of the development of my mind and character, manuscript autobiography, Darwin Online
Euclid: Elements, David Joyce edition
sources.note: Greek mathematical text in a modern explanatory edition. Diagram alone is not proof.

sources.title: From DNA to Beer, US National Library of Medicine
MacTutor: Leonardo Pisano Fibonacci
sources.note: Liber abaci (1202) and learning arithmetic in North Africa; not invention of Indian numerals.

sources.title: Ørsted compass needle, 1828 — Science Museum Group
sources.note: A surviving demonstration instrument, not a claim about a single dramatic discovery moment.

sources.title: Oersted’s experiment — Institute of Physics
sources.note: Supports opposite compass directions above and below a current-carrying wire. Construction and power-supply instructions deliberately excluded.

sources.title: Michael Faraday’s ring-coil apparatus — Royal Institution
sources.note: August 1831 apparatus and brief induced current in the other coil; object evidence anchors the reconstruction.

sources.title: John Graunt: Natural and Political Observations on the Bills of Mortality, 1662
sources.note: Primary text for population tabulation. Historical cause labels have uncertainty.

sources.title: Greek Sources in Arabic and Islamic Philosophy, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
Mark Schiefsky, The Creation of Second-Order Knowledge in Ancient Greek Science
OU primary-book exhibition: Harvey
sources.note: Harvey used quantitative, experimental, analogical and teleological arguments. Recipes isolate questions rather than reconstruct his whole reasoning.

sources.title: Siccar Point: geological evidence and Hutton
sources.note: Hutton used an unconformity to support an existing account of repeated geological processes; one scene does not establish every feature of his theory.

sources.title: Gysel: Vesalius’s Fabrica and the masticatory system
sources.note: Historical research contrasts the earlier Tabulae with the Fabrica’s account of a unified mandible. Adult anatomy; developmental fusion complicates an unqualified one-bone slogan.

sources.title: Museo Galileo: Kepler, Ad Vitellionem paralipomena
sources.note: Kepler revises inherited optics; telescope observation alone did not uniquely prove heliocentrism.

sources.title: Royal Museums Greenwich: Harrison and longitude
sources.note: Chronometers and lunar distances coexisted. Sea trials, cost and reproducibility matter alongside invention.

sources.title: Darwin Correspondence Project: Charles Lyell
sources.note: Documented geological influence with continuing disagreement, not blanket acceptance.

sources.title: Thomas Malthus: Essay on the Principle of Population, 1798
sources.note: The ratios are Malthus’s argumentative model, not a universal empirical law or moral instruction.

sources.title: Maths in the Early Islamic World, BBC synopsis reproduced by participant Peter Pormann / University of Manchester
Isaac Newton, General Scholium, 1729 English edition, Newton Project
NIST AI RMF Core
sources.note: Model validation, generalization limits and ongoing evaluation. A checklist is not a guarantee of trustworthiness.

sources.title: A. I. Sabra and Jan Hogendijk, The Optics of Ibn al-Haytham Books IV–V, Warburg Institute / University of Chicago Press
Cambridge Peterhouse MS209: Alhacen De Aspectibus
sources.note: A manuscript witness to the circulation of Ibn al-Haytham’s optical work. Optical recipes are modern demonstrations, not a transcription of this manuscript.

sources.title: Science Museum Group: Camera Obscura
sources.note: Historical portable camera obscura object. Does not establish every recipe or an exclusive inventor.

sources.title: Elinor Ostrom: Beyond Markets and States
sources.note: Institutional design is contextual; neither markets, states nor commons automatically solve every collective-action problem.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Personal Identity
sources.note: Philosophical distinctions and thought experiments; not evidence for uploading, artificial consciousness or a settled identity criterion.

sources.title: National Gallery: perspective
sources.note: Linear perspective is one historically specific representational practice, not the culmination of all painting.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Talbot and photography
sources.note: Several processes and contributors; a reproducible negative differs from a unique direct-positive image. No chemical procedure is taught.

sources.title: MIT 6.02 — Compression Algorithms, chapter 3
sources.note: Prefix-free code trees and expected length Σ pᵢℓᵢ. The ten-pair batch, 45-bit budget and all toy calculations are authored examples.

sources.title: Library of Congress: printing in Asia
sources.note: Collection-based context for coexisting block/type technologies. Our workshop orders and cost comparisons are fictional teaching cases, not historical data.

sources.title: Pascal–Fermat correspondence, 1654
sources.note: The interrupted-game problem is a case study, not the first human reasoning about chance.

sources.title: Smithsonian Libraries: 1482 printed Latin Euclid
sources.note: A specific printed geometric text and its Arabic–Latin lineage; no universal sole-transmission claim.

sources.title: MIT 16.36 — Channel Capacity and Coding, lectures 13/14
sources.note: Repetition coding, receiver majority decoding, rate cost and separate source/channel coding. Our one-flip bound is an explicitly authored teaching model, not a claim about all channels.

sources.title: Claude Shannon, A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits (1938), MIT-hosted copy
Shannon: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
sources.note: Information-theoretic quantities do not measure truth, significance or wisdom.

sources.title: UCLA: Snow’s grand experiment
sources.note: Compare water companies and denominators, not merely dots on a map. Observational comparisons have limitations.

sources.title: UCLA: Broad Street outbreak context
sources.note: Do not claim a map alone revealed the cause, or pump-handle removal alone ended an already declining outbreak.

sources.title: NLM: Andreas Vesalius
sources.note: The Fabrica both relied on and corrected Galen. This is not a rejection of every inherited account.

sources.title: Becker Medical Library: Vesalius in Italy and the Fabrica
sources.note: The production and printing of the 1543 Fabrica connected anatomical images, woodblocks and readers.

sources.title: Darwin Correspondence Project: Writing Origin
sources.note: Wallace’s independent 1858 work and joint presentation; not a single-contributor story.

sources.title: Aristotle, Posterior Analytics II.2 and II.8
sources.note: Primary text distinguishes the observed eclipse from inquiry into its cause, including Earth screening, rotation or extinction. The game dialogue and identical predictions are invented.

notes: Research candidate, new identity; old campaign and saves remain untouched.
One chronological route with braided returns; no new UI and no carried-item explanatory paragraphs.
All recipe examples are authored teaching cases, not verbatim historical texts. Completing a model reconstructs a position, not proof of its universal truth.
Scoped opening revision after negative blind trial: specific cases, terminal results, and limited evidence-order alternatives. No claim of improved enjoyment until a new trial.
